Introduction Anxiety disorders, as described in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), include several conditions: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), which is characterized by excessive and chronic worry. Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), marked by an extreme fear of social situations. Panic Disorder (PD), described as experiencing recurring panic attacks. Specific Phobia (SP), defined by intense fear or anxiety related to a specific object or situation 1 . Anxiety disorders are the most common type of mental health issue and significantly affect individuals’ quality of life and overall functioning 2 . Cognitive impairments are a significant area of research related to pathological anxiety and have been the subject of extensive studies 3 . Psychological distress often correlates with reduced cognitive and psychosocial functioning, and this decline can persist even after symptoms have subsided, negatively affecting the lives of those impacted 4 . Individuals diagnosed with anxiety disorders are 1.4 times more likely to drop out of high school, and approximately 50% of those with anxiety do not complete their high school education due to their condition 5 . Among various areas of cognitive impairment and dysfunction, anxiety is most closely linked to difficulties in selective attention and working memory (WM) 6 . Worry is significantly connected to deficits in WM’s capacity to filter out distracting threats, which may result in increased electrophysiological activity in regions associated with WM 7 – 9 . The possible connection between high anxiety and impaired working memory has captured the attention of numerous researchers in the field of psychology and neuroscience, leading to the development of various theoretical hypotheses. Some theories propose that anxiety directly causes deficits in working memory, suggesting that the heightened levels of stress and worry associated with anxiety interfere with cognitive processes 10 . In contrast, other theories suggest that excessive anxiety diminishes the efficiency of the central executive component of the working memory system, which is responsible for managing and coordinating cognitive tasks. This impairment can result in reduced attentional control, making it more challenging for individuals to focus on relevant information while filtering out distractions. Ultimately, this leads to a diminished capacity for working memory, which can significantly impact daily functioning and overall quality of life 11 , 12 . In addition to the idea that anxiety disrupts working memory, another perspective suggests the reverse relationship, proposing that working memory may actually contribute to anxiety. This theory of cognitive vulnerability to anxiety posits that the capacity of working memory plays a vital role in breaking the negative feedback loop of activated associations and attentional focus. Consequently, variations in working memory capacity could be a significant factor in determining an individual’s cognitive susceptibility to anxiety 13 , 14 . Taking into account the connection between anxiety and attention, research indicates that anxiety disorders may arise either from heightened activity in emotional affect networks or from difficulties in disengaging from negative thoughts due to issues within attention networks. Further research is essential to develop effective therapies and to explore whether treatments grounded in neuroscience principles could be beneficial for individuals with anxiety disorders 15 . Treating anxiety disorders with commonly prescribed medications, such as antidepressants, atypical antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, and tranquilizers, often does not lead to significant improvements in cognitive functions and may sometimes worsen the problems 3 . It is important to note that while pharmacological treatments, particularly first-line antidepressants like SSRIs and SNRIs, can effectively reduce anxiety, they tend to act slowly and rarely result in sustained remission 16 . Recent evidence suggests that cognitive interventions, broadly categorized as cognitive rehabilitation, training, and remediation, can lead to significant, though modest, enhancements in cognitive functions like memory, problem-solving, and attention in various mental health conditions. These interventions have proven beneficial for patients with mild cognitive impairment, schizophrenia, ADHD, and more 17 – 22 . Research indicates that cognitive training interventions can significantly enhance cognitive abilities in both healthy individuals and those with cognitive impairments. Furthermore, neuroimaging studies show that the brain exhibits plasticity from birth through late adulthood, suggesting that cognitive skills can be developed and improved at any stage of life through increased neuroplasticity 23 . To stimulate neuroplastic changes, cognitive training programs and neuromodulation methods are utilized. These strategies specifically target brain circuits, promote synaptic plasticity, and enhance cognitive functions 24 . Despite increasing interest in cognitive rehabilitation, especially working memory and attention training, the evidence in anxiety disorders remains scattered. Prior reviews have either focused on non-clinical groups or specific cognitive domains, leaving uncertainty about their clinical relevance 25 , 26 . Therefore, a systematic review that combines available evidence in adults with anxiety disorders is needed to clarify the effectiveness and limitations of these interventions. In this study, we sought to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of research that utilized cognitive rehabilitation to enhance cognitive functions and alleviate symptoms in adult patients with anxiety disorders. The aim is to assess the quality of evidence and the effectiveness of cognitive rehabilitation in addressing various cognitive functions and reducing the severity of anxiety symptoms. Methods Eligibility This article adheres to the standards set by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 27 and is registered in PROSPERO repository (registration number: [CRD42024508413]). The PRISMA 2020 checklist, detailing how each reporting item was addressed in the manuscript, is available in Supplementary Material 1. The participants in the studies included in this systematic review and meta-analysis were all at least 18 years old. They had either been clinically diagnosed with an anxiety disorder, based on established criteria from the 5th edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) 28 , or had scores that exceeded the threshold on standardized assessment scales. Studies involving subclinical participants were not included in the review. Additionally, the review did not cover any research focused on pediatric or geriatric populations. In line with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, our eligibility criteria can be summarized according to the PICO framework: Population: adults (≥ 18 years) with a primary diagnosis of an anxiety disorder; Intervention: cognitive training interventions targeting working memory or attention; Comparison: passive controls (e.g., waitlist, sham training) or active controls (e.g., relaxation, non-adaptive training); Outcomes: validated measures of anxiety symptoms and related cognitive outcomes. The selected studies included participants who did not have any diagnosed neurodegenerative diseases, such as dementia or multiple system atrophy, nor any neurological conditions, including Parkinson’s disease or traumatic brain injury. In other words, the cognitive impairments observed in the participants were solely attributed to anxiety. Additionally, we excluded articles that recruited participants with major psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia or major depressive disorder (MDD), as well as studies focusing on specific neuropsychiatric conditions like stroke. For studies with mixed diagnostic groups—such as patients with various anxiety disorders alongside those diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) or MDD—we included the research only if we could extract data specifically related to patients with an anxiety disorder diagnosis from the study reports. The study focused on research projects that investigated the effects of cognitive remediation, cognitive rehabilitation, and cognitive training. It excluded studies that evaluated any other treatments, whether pharmacological or non-pharmacological, such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, Attention Bias Modification (ABM), or any meta-cognitive interventions. Participants were either medication-free or, if on stable pharmacological treatment, were required to maintain unchanged dosage throughout the trial period. Eligible studies included controlled randomized clinical trials that involved at least two groups of qualified participants. If multiple scales were available for the same variable, we selected the instrument most widely validated and recognized in clinical anxiety research as the reference measure (e.g., LSAS for social anxiety, PSWQ for generalized anxiety, STAI for general anxiety symptoms). If all scales were equally standard, the one shared with other studies was selected. These studies assessed pre- and post-intervention measures in at least one domain related to anxiety or cognition. Exclusion criteria during full-text screening included: (i) studies involving subclinical populations, (ii) mixed diagnoses without extractable anxiety disorder data, (iii) use of non-cognitive rehabilitation interventions (e.g., CBT, ABM), (iv) absence of a control group, (v) lack of pre- and post-intervention cognitive or symptom severity outcomes, and (vi) non-randomized designs. Search strategy and study selection We conducted a search using databases such as PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Cochrane, and Proquest, in collaboration with an expert research librarian. Our focus was on selecting controlled and randomized trials (blinded or not) published before June 2024. The search process and the terms employed in our systematic review are shown in Table 1 , and the complete Boolean search strings for each database are provided in Supplementary Material 2. Table 1 Search strategy and key Words. Question Keywords Patients: Adults with anxiety disorders Anxiety disorders; Social anxiety disorder; Social phobia; Specific phobia; Panic disorder; Generalized anxiety disorder; SAD; SP; PD; GAD; MeSH term: ‘Anxiety Disorders’; MeSH term: ‘Social Anxiety Disorder’; MeSH term: ‘Panic Disorder’; MeSH term: ‘Phobic Disorders’; ‘general anxiety disorder’ Intervention: Cognitive rehabilitation Cognitive rehabilitation; Cognitive remediation; Cognitive training; Computerized cognitive rehabilitation; Computerized cognitive remediation; Computerized cognitive training; Cognitive dysfunction/rehabilitation; Cognitive remediation/methods; Cognitive remediation/standards; Computer-assisted instruction; CRT; CR; Neurocognitive rehabilitation; Neuropsychological rehabilitation; MeSH term: ‘Cognitive Rehabilitation’; MeSH term: ‘Cognitive Therapy’ Comparison: Control group with same disorder Randomized controlled trial; Clinical trial; Randomized trial; Randomized controlled clinical trial; Randomized controlled trials as topic; RCT; Control group; Wait-list control; Active control; Sham control Outcome: Improving cognitive deficits and symptom severity Cognitive deficit; Cognitive dysfunction; Cognitive impairment; Cognition; Attention; Processing speed; Executive function; Working memory; Verbal memory; Verbal fluency; Visuospatial memory; Neuropsychological testing; Neuropsychological tests; Neuropsychological cognitive testing; Cognitive anxiety disorders diagnosis; MeSH term: ‘Attention’; MeSH term: ‘Working Memory’ We also assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach across five domains: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Certainty was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low 29 . The GRADE assessment is presented in the Supplementary Material 3. Two reviewers (SM, AM) independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or adjudication by a third reviewer (MS). Data extraction was also performed in duplicate and cross-checked for accuracy. Data analysis We utilized Comprehensive Meta-Analysis Software (version 3) in order to conduct this meta-analysis 30 . We calculated the standardized mean differences using a random effects model, along with a 95% confidence interval for the changes in outcome measures from baseline to post-intervention between the cognitive rehabilitation and control groups. The analysis included symptom severity of anxiety disorders and cognitive functions as outcome measures. Standard assessments for anxiety symptoms and objective standardized cognitive tests were deemed eligible as outcomes. Cognitive functions were categorized into standard cognitive domains, and any domain that was used in more than two studies was included in the analysis. In cases where there were more than two groups, the ‘shared’ group was subdivided into two or more smaller groups, enabling independent comparisons to be made. The definitions for weighted mean effect sizes were as follows: 0.2 to 0.49 was considered small, 0.5 to 0.79 was medium, and greater than 0.8 was classified as large 31 . The chi-square statistic and I² calculation were employed to assess heterogeneity among the studies. An I² value of less than 40% was classified as small, 30–60% as moderate, 50–90% as substantial, and greater than 75% as considerable heterogeneity 32 . Additionally, we conducted sensitivity analysis and/or subgroup analysis to address clinical heterogeneity. We evaluated the risk of six main biases using the Cochrane “Risk of Bias” tool 33 . Two reviewers (SM and MS) independently assessed the risk of bias for each included study. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. Following Cochrane recommendations, funnel plots were generated for descriptive purposes only, as fewer than 10 studies were included in the meta-analyses. Therefore, the visual assessment of potential publication bias should be interpreted with caution. Results Study characteristics The database search identified a total of 1,825 studies of interest, from which 147 duplicates were initially removed. This left 1,678 records, and after evaluating the titles and abstracts, 1,648 studies were excluded. Out of the 30 full-text articles reviewed, eight studies met the inclusion criteria and were deemed eligible for further analysis (see Fig. 1 , and Supplementary Material 4). These eight studies involved a total of 242 participants in the cognitive rehabilitation group and 223 participants in the control group. Among the eligible studies, three focused on attention training techniques (ATT), while five assessed working memory training (WMT). Four studies evaluated the effectiveness of cognitive rehabilitation in adult patients with social anxiety disorder (SAD), and the remaining four examined adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). All eligible studies reported data on the severity of symptoms related to anxiety disorders; three studies reported on participants’ attention, and three studies reported on working memory. Symptom severity Eight studies involving 242 patients in the cognitive intervention group and 223 in the control group evaluated the severity of symptoms related to anxiety disorders and provided the necessary data. The meta-analysis of these results showed a significant difference between the intervention and control groups, with an effect size of 0.25 (95% CI, 0.02 to 0.47), a p-value of 0.02, and an I² value of 30.12%. The forest plot illustrating the anxiety disorder symptom severity analyses is shown in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 The forest plot of analyses of the symptom severity of anxiety disorders. Cognitive functions After reviewing all the included studies, we focused on analyzing attention and working memory. The meta-analysis of three studies, which assessed the attention of 61 patients in the cognitive rehabilitation group and 83 patients in the control group, found no significant difference between the two groups. The results indicated a difference of 0.07 (95% CI, −0.25 to 0.4), with a p-value of 0.65 and an I² statistic of 0.00%. The forest plot representing the analysis of the attention is displayed in Fig. 3 . Fig. 3 The forest plot of analyses of the attention. The meta-analysis of three studies evaluated the working memory of 108 patients in the cognitive intervention group and 70 patients in the control group, resulting in an I² of 64.12%. Consequently, we employed the random effects model for our analysis. The results indicated a significant difference between the two groups, with a moderate effect size of 0.6 (95% CI: 0.07 to 1.13; p-value = 0.02). The forest plot illustrating the analyses of working memory is presented in Fig. 4 , while the funnel plot is shown in Fig. 5 . Given that fewer than 10 studies were included in this meta-analysis, the funnel plot should be considered descriptive and does not permit a robust assessment of publication bias. Fig. 4 The forest plot pf the working memory. Fig. 5 The funnel plot of the working memory. As indicated by the plots, a sensitivity analysis (remove-one analysis) revealed that the study by du Toit et al. 36 contained outlier data. When this study was excluded from the meta-analysis, the results remained significant, showing an even larger effect size of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.47 to 1.21; p-value < 0.001; I² = 0.00%). The forest plot for this revised analysis is displayed in Fig. 6 . Fig. 6 The forest plot of analyses of the working memory after sensitivity analysis. Subgroup analysis Diagnosis We conducted a sub-group analysis on symptom severity to assess the impact of specific anxiety disorder diagnoses (Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)). Our analysis examined data from four studies involving 82 patients diagnosed with SAD in the cognitive rehabilitation group and 92 patients in the control group. The analysis yielded an I² value of 48.32%. Given this, we utilized a random effects model for our evaluation. The results indicated no significant difference in symptom severity between the two groups, with a mean difference of 0.22 (95% Confidence Interval: −0.2 to 0.65; p-value = 0.29). The forest plot illustrating these analyses is presented in Fig. 7 , while the funnel plot is shown in Fig. 8 . Given that fewer than 10 studies were included in this meta-analysis, the funnel plot should be considered descriptive and does not permit a robust assessment of publication bias. Fig. 7 The forest plot of the symptom severity of SAD. Fig. 8 The funnel plot of the symptom severity of SAD. A meta-analysis of data from four studies involving 160 patients with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) in the cognitive rehabilitation group and 131 patients in the control group found no significant difference in symptom severity between the two groups. The mean difference was 0.26 (95% Confidence Interval: −0.2 to 0.55, p-value = 0.07, I² = 28.82%). The Fig. 9 presents a forest plot illustrating these analyses. Fig. 9 The forest plot of the symptom severity of GAD. Intervention We performed a sub-group analysis on cognitive functions and the symptom severity of anxiety disorders to determine the effect of the model of intervention ATT and WMT. The meta-analysis of three studies evaluating ATT did not show a significant difference in symptom severity of anxiety disorders between cognitive rehabilitation and control groups (0.05 (95% CI: −0.2 to 0.31; p-value = 0.66; I² = 0.00%). The forest plot representing this analysis is displayed in Fig. 10 . Fig. 10 The forest plot of the symptom severity in ATT intervention. Two of the three studies evaluating ATT provided data on participants’ cognitive functions. The analysis of these two studies did not reveal a significant difference in cognitive functions related to anxiety disorders between the cognitive rehabilitation group and the control group (mean difference: 0.07; 95% CI: −0.34 to 0.5; p-value = 0.72; I² = 20.08%). The forest plot illustrating this analysis is displayed in Fig. 11 . Fig. 11 The forest plot of the cognitive functions in ATT intervention. In contrast, the meta-analysis of five studies evaluating WMT showed a significant difference in the symptom severity of anxiety disorders between the cognitive rehabilitation group and the control group (mean difference: 0.41; 95% CI: −0.08 to 0.74; p-value = 0.01; I² = 32.65%). The forest plot representing these analyses is presented in Fig. 12 , and the funnel plot in Fig. 13 . Given that fewer than 10 studies were included in this meta-analysis, the funnel plot should be considered descriptive and does not permit a robust assessment of publication bias. Fig. 12 The forest plot of the symptom severity in WMT intervention. Fig. 13 The funnel plot of the symptom severity in WMT intervention. Four of the five studies assessing WMT reported data on participants’ cognitive functions. The analysis yielded an I² value of 61.16%, leading us to utilize a random effects model for our evaluation. The results indicated a significant difference in cognitive functions between the two groups, with a mean difference of 0.49 (95% CI: 0.02 to 0.97; p-value = 0.03). The forest plot illustrating these analyses is shown in Fig. 14 , and the funnel plot is shown in Fig. 15 . Given that fewer than 10 studies were included in this meta-analysis, the funnel plot should be considered descriptive and does not permit a robust assessment of publication bias. Fig. 14 The forest plot of the cognitive functions in WMT intervention. Fig. 15 The funnel plot of the cognitive functions in WMT intervention. To address the heterogeneity observed, we evaluated the funnel plot of this data. The plots indicated that two studies contained outlier data. Since these studies had approximately equal weight and standard residuals in the analysis, we decided to remove both Zhao et al. 37 and du Toit et al. 36 from further consideration. After excluding these studies from the meta-analysis, the results remained significant, yielding an effect size of 0.51 (95% CI: 0.09 to 0.93; p-value = 0.01; I² = 15.22%). The forest plot for this revised analysis is displayed in Fig. 16 . Fig. 16 The funnel plot of the symptom severity in WMT intervention after sensitivity analysis. Risk of bias The evaluation of the risk of bias in the studies for six main biases revealed that the overall quality of the studies was high. The results of this evaluation are illustrated in Fig. 17 . A full tabular presentation of RoB 2 domain-level judgments and all signaling question responses for each included study is provided in Supplementary Material 5. Fig. 17 The assessment of the main biases of the studies. Discussion We conducted this systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the effectiveness of cognitive rehabilitation in reducing symptom severity and improving cognitive functions in adult patients with anxiety disorders. Our findings indicate that cognitive rehabilitation is an effective intervention for reducing symptom severity and enhancing working memory in patients with anxiety disorders. However, current cognitive rehabilitation therapies do not effectively improve attention. A systematic search strategy identified a significantly more significant number of studies on this topic, totaling 1,825. However, only eight of these articles were standardized randomized clinical trials that included a control group and focused on adult patients with clinically diagnosed anxiety disorders. The exclusion of many studies involving subclinical anxiety patients indicates that cognitive rehabilitation is not a primary focus in the treatment of clinically diagnosed anxiety disorders. Another reason for the significant number of exclusions in studies is the predominant focus on maladaptive patterns and biases related to cognitive functions, such as cognitive bias modification. This emphasis often overlooks cognitive rehabilitation, which takes a more comprehensive approach by concentrating on specific neural pathways and promoting neuroplasticity. According to this review, current cognitive rehabilitation therapies significantly reduce the severity of anxiety disorder symptoms, with a small effect size of 0.25. No previous reviews or meta-analyses have evaluated this matter. Our subgroup analysis revealed differences based on the type of intervention. Our results indicate that the ATT was ineffective in reducing the severity of anxiety disorder symptoms. In contrast, WMT effectively decreased symptom severity in patients, demonstrating a moderate effect size. Previous reviews, which included case series, case reports, and nonrandomized trials, suggested that ATT might be effective in reducing the severity of anxiety symptoms 41 , 42 . This first meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials showed no significant difference in the severity of anxiety symptoms between the ATT and control groups. Our findings align with a meta-analysis conducted on the anxiety-reducing effects of WMT. Wang et al. 25 reported that WMT had a small but statistically significant impact on the severity of anxiety symptoms. Despite obtaining similar results, there are several noteworthy differences between our study and that of Wang et al. Wang et al. evaluated the anxiety-reducing effects of WMT but did not focus on patients with anxiety disorders. They did not apply any inclusion criteria regarding whether participants had undergone screening for baseline anxiety or had received a diagnosis of anxiety disorders. Additionally, there were no exclusion criteria for any medical or psychiatric comorbidities. Considering these differences and comparing the small effect size found in the study by Wang et al. to the moderate effect size observed in our study, it seems reasonable to suggest that WMT may be more effective in reducing anxiety clinically anxious patients compared to other populations. In our analysis of the cognitive functions of adult patients with anxiety disorders, we found that cognitive rehabilitation significantly enhances working memory, although this conclusion is based on a small number of heterogeneous studies and should be interpreted cautiously. Sensitivity analysis suggests the effect may be driven by a few studies, highlighting the need for replication in larger trials. Additionally, our subgroup analysis supported these findings differently. Specifically, when analyzing the type of intervention, we discovered that WMT significantly enhanced the cognitive functions of adults with anxiety disorders. In contrast, there was no significant difference in cognitive functions between the ATT and the control groups. Our findings align with the extensive research that identifies working memory (WM) as a crucial explanatory factor in anxiety models 5 , 10 , 11 , 43 – 46 . Specifically, the cognitive vulnerability model that suggests the working memory deficits observed in patients with anxiety may be a significant contributor to clinical anxiety rather than merely a result of perceived threats 47 . According to this theory, working memory training can successfully improve working memory capacity by repeatedly practicing cognitive tasks that have high working memory demands. This increased capacity provides more resources to manage anxiety, resulting in a reduction of anxiety symptoms 25 . Several factors may explain why cognitive rehabilitation did not enhance attention in adults with anxiety disorders and why ATT showed no significant improvement in their cognitive functions. One possible reason is the limited number of studies available. Only two studies 34 , 38 that evaluated ATT included data on cognitive outcomes, with 48 patients in the intervention group and 70 in the control group. In contrast, multiple studies have demonstrated the positive effects of attention bias modification therapy on anxiety disorders 18 , 48 , 49 , and attention bias models have been effective in explaining the psychopathology associated with some of these disorders 50 . It’s possible that improvements in the symptoms of patients with anxiety disorders—unlike working memory, as highlighted in our findings—may be achieved through the modification of threat-related attention rather than through a general enhancement of attention itself. We conducted a subgroup analysis to evaluate symptom severity and its relationship with specific anxiety disorder diagnoses. Our findings indicated no significant difference in symptom severity of the GAD and SAD groups compared to the control groups. However, a separate analysis based on the type of intervention revealed that WMT effectively reduced symptoms in patients with anxiety disorders, regardless of their specific diagnosis. In contrast, patients in the ATT intervention groups did not show a significant difference in symptom severity compared to the control group. One explanation for our findings may be the limited number of studies available. The small sample size likely contributed to the diminished power in our subgroup analysis. However, when we combine the diagnostic and intervention analysis results, we can derive interesting interpretations. It appears that cognitive rehabilitation may help reduce symptom severity in adults with anxiety disorders by targeting specific neurocognitive deficits. For instance, our findings suggest that improving working memory is associated with a decrease in symptom severity among anxious participants. In contrast, targeting attention not only failed to lead to symptom improvement but also did not enhance attention deficits. These non-significant findings may partly reflect methodological limitations, including small sample sizes and heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria, intervention protocols, and outcome measures across studies 34 , 36 , 38 . Moreover, theoretical models suggest that attention and working memory may relate to anxiety through distinct mechanisms. While impaired working memory capacity may directly limit the resources available for regulating anxious thoughts 10 , 11 , 25 , 47 , attentional impairments in anxiety may instead reflect biases toward threat-related stimuli 48 – 50 . Thus, interventions targeting general attentional control may not sufficiently address the mechanisms most relevant to symptom change. The evaluation of the included studies indicated high quality. Since we only considered randomized controlled trials, these areas are free from biases. All the studies utilized appropriate and targeted scales to assess symptom severity and cognitive functions. Given the low heterogeneity and minimal risk of bias across all studies, the results can be deemed reliable and conclusive. However, due to the limited number of studies included, the interpretations should be approached with caution. Although heterogeneity across interventions, participant demographics, and outcome measures was already described in the Results and considered in analysis, this variability is likely one of factors contributed to inconsistent findings across studies and may limit the generalizability of the pooled estimates. One significant limitation of this study is the narrow range of diagnoses assessed. Only GAD and SAD were included. Furthermore, most studies that examined GAD relied on standard diagnostic scales rather than clinical interviews and evaluations by mental health professionals. There are currently no studies available that evaluate panic disorder and specific phobia. This limitation also applies to the interventions addressing targeted cognitive deficits. Currently, only WMT and ATT have been evaluated in a limited number of studies. Other cognitive deficits, such as various executive functions and specific aspects of memory and attention—including visual, verbal, and procedural memory, as well as selective and shifting attention—have not been assessed in adults with anxiety disorders. Another limitation is that none of the studies evaluating cognitive rehabilitation for adults with anxiety disorders have follow-up measures. In addition to the clear importance of assessing if the effects of cognitive rehabilitation persist over time, follow-up assessments can help identify the various factors contributing to these treatment outcomes. For example, improvements observed in many studies may stem from increased self-efficacy and self-esteem gained from participating in cognitive rehabilitation programs and the confidence that comes from successfully completing structured cognitive tasks. Consequently, these effects may not be evident in later assessments. In summary, this review has several limitations. First, the number of eligible studies was small, which restricted the statistical power of the analyses and limited the ability to conduct robust subgroup comparisons. Second, there was considerable heterogeneity across studies in terms of participant demographics, intervention protocols, training duration, and outcome measures, which complicates interpretation and reduces generalizability. Third, most of the included trials were conducted with relatively small sample sizes, which increases the uncertainty of pooled estimates. In addition, most studies did not include follow-up assessments, limiting conclusions about the durability of intervention effects. The evidence also lacks studies targeting other anxiety disorders, such as panic disorder or specific phobia, reducing the scope of applicability. Finally, potential placebo or expectancy effects related to participation in structured cognitive tasks cannot be fully ruled out. Future studies should consider these factors. Additional research is necessary across various anxiety diagnoses, incorporating clinical psychiatric evaluations and distinguishing detailed cognitive deficits. Multiple targeted interventions and follow-up measurements should also be included. Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrate that cognitive rehabilitation is an effective intervention for reducing symptom severity and improving working memory in patients with anxiety disorders. Given the significance of achieving complete remission from these disorders and addressing the neuropsychological deficits associated with anxiety, cognitive rehabilitation should be regarded as an essential component of treatment for anxious patients. Further research focusing on different anxiety diagnoses, cognitive deficits, and targeted interventions is necessary. documents.title: The impact of fluoxetine on obesity and diabetes-related biomarkers in overweight and obese individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
documents.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), is widely used in clinical practice for managing depression and anxiety. Emerging evidence suggests fluoxetine may influence body weight (BW) and glucose metabolism, yet its potential benefits in overweight or obese individuals remain unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the impact of fluoxetine on obesity-related parameters and diabetes-related biomarkers in overweight and obese adults. METHODS: We systematically searched four major databases (Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and PubMed/MEDLINE) following PRISMA guidelines for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effects of fluoxetine on BW, fasting blood sugar (FBS), and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in overweight or obese individuals. Data were pooled using a random-effects model, and subgroup analyses were conducted based on fluoxetine dose, intervention duration, and obesity classification. RESULTS: Results: A total of 26 RCTs met the inclusion criteria. Fluoxetine administration was associated with a significant reduction in BW (WMD: − 2.095 kg; 95% CI: − 2.806 to − 1.385; p  12 weeks), especially among obese individuals (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²). CONCLUSIONS: Fluoxetine was associated with modest but statistically significant reductions in BW, FBS, and HbA1c levels in overweight and obese individuals. The greatest weight loss was observed at doses ≥ 60 mg/day over shorter durations (≤ 12 weeks), whereas greater reductions in HbA1c were seen in longer trials (> 12 weeks) at similar dosages.

Data were pooled using a random-effects model, and subgroup analyses were conducted based on fluoxetine dose, intervention duration, and obesity classification. Results Results: A total of 26 RCTs met the inclusion criteria. Fluoxetine administration was associated with a significant reduction in BW (WMD: − 2.095 kg; 95% CI: − 2.806 to − 1.385; p < 0.001), particularly at doses ≥ 60 mg/day and in studies lasting ≤ 12 weeks. FBS (WMD: − 8.70 mg/dL; 95% CI: − 17.25 to − 0.14; p = 0.046) and HbA1c (WMD: − 0.61%; 95% CI: − 1.22 to − 0.016; p = 0.044) also decreased significantly. Notably, while BW reduction was greater in shorter trials (≤ 12 weeks), HbA1c improvement was more pronounced in longer trials (> 12 weeks), especially among obese individuals (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²). Conclusions Fluoxetine was associated with modest but statistically significant reductions in BW, FBS, and HbA1c levels in overweight and obese individuals. The greatest weight loss was observed at doses ≥ 60 mg/day over shorter durations (≤ 12 weeks), whereas greater reductions in HbA1c were seen in longer trials (> 12 weeks) at similar dosages. Introduction Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most commonly recommended class of antidepressants due to their generally favorable side effect profiles compared to other medications [ 1 ]. Among SSRIs, fluoxetine is frequently prescribed for managing mental health conditions [ 2 ]. Beyond their antidepressant effects, SSRIs have also shown promise in supporting long-term neural recovery after ischemic stroke and in managing blood pressure, blood glucose, and lipid profiles [ 3 ]. However, side effects such as dyslipidemia and weight gain are frequently reported and often lead to early discontinuation of treatment [ 4 ]. While weight gain is a well-documented side effect of many SSRIs, fluoxetine appears to be an exception in some cases. Evidence indicates that fluoxetine may promote weight loss or mitigate weight gain, particularly during the early stages of treatment [ 5 ]. This contrasts with other SSRIs, which more commonly contribute to weight gain over time. The variability in weight-related outcomes across SSRIs is likely attributable to differences in their pharmacodynamic profiles, especially their selective action on serotonin pathways [ 6 ]. Despite significant progress in treating obesity-related comorbidities such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia, the development of effective anti-obesity medications has lagged. Given the rising prevalence of obesity and increased public health focus, there is strong interest in developing effective pharmaceutical interventions [ 7 ]. One promising avenue is based on findings that serotonin levels in the medial hypothalamus affect appetite, meal timing, caloric intake, and carbohydrate cravings [ 8 ]. Fluoxetine, an SSRI, has attracted attention for its potential influence on these behaviors [ 9 ]. Unlike tricyclic antidepressants, which may promote weight gain possibly via their effects on norepinephrine in the medial hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, fluoxetine acts selectively on serotonin reuptake [ 10 ]. By enhancing serotonergic activity, fluoxetine may influence eating behaviors and body weight (BW), a hypothesis supported by evidence from both animal and human studies [ 6 ]. Abdominal obesity, in particular, is associated with a heightened risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) [ 11 ]. Multiple studies have demonstrated that increased visceral fat correlates with elevated glucose and insulin levels [ 12 , 13 ]. Fluoxetine may exert beneficial effects on fasting blood glucose and serum insulin, independent of weight loss, potentially reducing the risk of coronary heart disease and T2DM [ 14 ]. Given these observations, it is important to assess the impact of fluoxetine on both obesity and diabetes-related biomarkers in overweight and obese individuals. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to assess the effects of fluoxetine on key outcomes, including body weight (BW), fasting blood sugar (FBS), and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), in this population. Materials and methods Study design and literature search This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 15 ]. A comprehensive search strategy was implemented across multiple electronic databases—Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and PubMed/MEDLINE, from their inception through September 4, 2024. The search was unrestricted by language or publication date. To ensure the inclusion of all relevant studies, both free-text terms and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) were employed, as detailed in Supplementary Table 1. Additionally, manual screening of the reference lists of pertinent articles was performed to identify further eligible trials. Eligibility criteria The selection of studies was guided by the Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome (PICO) framework. Studies were deemed eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: (1) Population: adults (aged ≥ 18 years) classified as overweight or obese (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m²), (2) Intervention: administration of fluoxetine, (3) Comparator: a placebo group, and (4) Outcome: reported mean and standard deviation (SD) of body mass index (BMI), BW, and/or waist circumference (WC) at both baseline and the end of the intervention. Studies were excluded if they were conference abstracts, lacked a control group, were not randomized controlled trials (RCTs), or did not provide sufficient outcome data for analysis. Data extraction Data from the included trials were independently extracted by two reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion with the corresponding author to reach consensus. Extracted variables included: fluoxetine dosage, duration of the intervention, year of publication, baseline and post-intervention means ± SD for each outcome, first author’s name, participants’ health status, country of study, average age, and sample size. Risk of bias assessment The methodological quality of the included RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool (RoB 2) [ 16 ]. This tool evaluates potential sources of bias across five domains: bias arising from the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported results. In addition, the strength of the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, which classifies certainty as very low, low, moderate, or high [ 17 ]. Statistical analysis Pooled effect estimates were calculated using the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model. Results were expressed as weighted mean differences (WMDs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). When studies did not provide standard deviations (SDs) for mean changes, or instead reported only standard errors (SEs) or 95% confidence intervals (CIs), the missing values were derived using established statistical methods [ 18 , 19 ]. SEs were converted to SDs with the formula SD = SE × √n, while SDs from 95% CIs were estimated using SD = (upper limit – lower limit)/(2 × 1.96) × √n. If SDs for net changes were not directly reported, they were calculated using the formula: SD change = √[(SDpre)² + (SDpost)² – (2 × R × SDpre × SDpost)], where R represents the correlation coefficient between pre- and post-intervention values. Following prior methodological recommendations, a correlation coefficient of 0.5 was assumed. Between-study heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q test and quantified by the I² statistic, with thresholds of > 50% indicating high heterogeneity, 26–50% indicating moderate heterogeneity, and < 25% indicating low heterogeneity. A P-value of less than 0.10 for the Q test was considered indicative of significant heterogeneity. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were performed to explore sources of heterogeneity, including the influence of fluoxetine dosage, baseline BMI, and duration of treatment on outcomes. Although participants’ health status (psychiatric vs. non-psychiatric populations) was considered, insufficient stratified data prevented us from conducting a reliable analysis on this variable. Publication bias was assessed through visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger’s regression test, with a P-value < 0.1 indicating potential bias [ 20 ]. Sensitivity analyses were conducted by sequentially omitting individual studies and recalculating the overall estimates to evaluate the robustness of the findings. All statistical analyses were conducted using Stata software, version 14 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA), with a two-tailed P-value < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results Study selection The initial database search identified 16,263 records. After removing 3,372 duplicates, 12,845 articles were excluded based on the screening of titles and abstracts due to irrelevance. A total of 46 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Following thorough evaluation, 26 studies [ 21 – 45 ] met the inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the meta-analysis. These included 22 RCT arms reporting on BW outcomes, 11 on FBS, 8 on HbA1c, and 6 on insulin levels (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Flowchart depicting the study selection and inclusion processes for the present meta-analysis RCT, randomized controlled trial(s) Characteristics of the included studies The selected RCTs were conducted across a wide geographical spectrum, including China, Iraq, Brazil, Denmark, the United States, Belgium, Canada, South Africa, Scotland, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom. The publication years of these studies ranged from 1987 to 2018. Participants’ mean ages spanned from 18 to 67 years, reflecting a broad adult population. The clinical populations investigated in these studies varied and included individuals with acute ischemic stroke, obese adults, premenopausal women with obesity, patients with type 1 diabetes, women diagnosed with major depressive disorder (according to DSM-IV criteria), outpatients with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder exhibiting early symptoms, adults with major depressive disorder, former smokers with biochemically validated nicotine abstinence, obese patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM), elderly individuals with diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, women with obesity and carbohydrate cravings, and men with central (abdominal) obesity. Intervention durations ranged from 11 days to 12 months, with fluoxetine administered in daily doses typically varying between 20 mg and 60 mg. Comprehensive details regarding the characteristics of the included trials are presented in Table 1 . The risk of bias assessment is summarized in Supplementary Table 2. Overall, the methodological quality of the included trials was generally good. Out of the 26 RCTs, 22 were rated as “good,” 2 as “fair,” and 1 as “poor” based on AHRQ standards. Most studies demonstrated low risk of bias for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome assessment. However, the study rated as “poor” quality (Connolly et al.) had concerns related to incomplete outcome data and reporting. These findings suggest that, while the majority of included trials were of high quality, the presence of a few lower-quality studies may have contributed to the observed heterogeneity. According to the GRADE assessment, fluoxetine showed a moderate certainty of evidence for reducing body weight, low certainty for lowering fasting blood sugar and HbA1c, and very low certainty for effects on insulin. Most outcomes were downgraded due to high heterogeneity, imprecision, and limited sample sizes (Supplementary Table 3). Several studies also noted weight change and sexual dysfunction as treatment-emergent effects. Discontinuation rates varied between trials but were generally attributed to tolerability concerns, with withdrawal most frequently due to nausea, insomnia, or anxiety. Importantly, the majority of studies concluded that fluoxetine was overall well tolerated, with adverse events typically mild to moderate in severity and comparable to placebo or control treatments. Findings from the Meta-Analysis Effect of Fluoxetine on body weight (BW) The pooled analysis, which included 22 RCT arms with a total of 2,348 participants (placebo: 1,166; fluoxetine: 1,182), demonstrated a significant reduction in BW with fluoxetine treatment (WMD: − 2.05 kg; 95% CI: − 2.74 to − 1.35; p < 0.001), as shown in Fig. 2 . A high degree of heterogeneity was detected among the included studies (I² = 84.2%, p < 0.001). Subgroup analysis indicated greater weight reduction with higher dosages (≥ 60 mg/day) (WMD: − 2.77 kg; 95% CI: − 3.60 to − 1.92; p < 0.001) compared to lower doses (< 60 mg/day) (WMD: − 1.02 kg; 95% CI: − 1.55 to − 0.50; p < 0.001). Furthermore, trials with shorter durations (≤ 12 weeks) demonstrated a more pronounced effect (WMD: − 3.000 kg; 95% CI: − 3.80 to − 2.18; p < 0.001) than those extending beyond 12 weeks (WMD: − 1.10 kg; 95% CI: − 2.13 to − 0.071; p = 0.036). Significant weight reduction was also observed in obese individuals (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²) (WMD: − 2.246 kg; 95% CI: − 3.425 to − 1.068; p < 0.001) compared to overweight participants (BMI 25–29.99 kg/m²) (WMD: − 1.972 kg; 95% CI: − 2.924 to − 1.021; p < 0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 1). Body weight (kg) was positively associated with treatment duration (Coef. = 0.045, p = 0.040) but negatively associated with fluoxetine dose (Coef. = −0.056, p = 0.011), suggesting that longer treatment duration slightly increased body weight, whereas higher fluoxetine doses were associated with a modest reduction in body weight. In contrast, f asting blood sugar (FBS, mg/dL) was not significantly associated with treatment duration (Coef. = −0.29, p = 0.319) or fluoxetine dose (Coef. = −0.312, p = 0.361). Similarly, HbA1c (%) showed no significant associations with treatment duration (Coef. = −0.031, p = 0.070) or fluoxetine dose (Coef. = −0.022, p = 0.394). Insulin levels (pmol/L) were also not significantly related to treatment duration (Coef. = −0.64, p = 0.639) or fluoxetine dose (Coef. = −0.425, p = 0.721) (Supplementary Fig. 2). Overall, these results suggest that while body weight may be influenced by both treatment duration and fluoxetine dose, glycemic parameters, including FBS, HbA1c, and insulin, appear largely unaffected by these factors in the included studies. Sensitivity analysis To evaluate the robustness of the meta-analytic findings, sensitivity analyses were conducted by systematically excluding each trial arm. These analyses indicated that the overall results were consistent and not substantially influenced by the removal of any single study (Supplementary Fig. 3). Publication bias Assessment of publication bias using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test did not reveal any significant asymmetry for the outcomes related to BW, FBS, HbA1c, or insulin, indicating a low likelihood of publication bias (Supplementary Fig. 4). Discussion Visceral fat accumulation—regardless of overall obesity level, is linked to elevated blood glucose levels. A medication that both promotes weight loss and improves glycemic control would be especially beneficial in managing abdominal obesity [ 46 ]. Our meta-analysis of RCTs examining fluoxetine’s effects on obesity and diabetes-related biomarkers found significant reductions in BW, FBS, and HbA1c, following fluoxetine treatment. Treatment regimens varied widely in dosage, duration, and comparator groups, and differences in obesity classification and diagnostic criteria contributed to heterogeneity across studies. Our analysis suggests that fluoxetine at doses ≥ 60 mg/day for ≤ 12 weeks leads to moderate BW reductions (~ 2.25–3 kg), particularly in individuals with a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m². Although the exact mechanism remains unclear, fluoxetine may reduce hunger by inhibiting neuropeptide Y and potentially increase resting energy expenditure [ 47 ]. Previous studies have reported weight loss in patients receiving SSRIs for acute conditions [ 48 ], and one meta-analysis found that adults taking fluoxetine lost an average of 1.3 kg [ 49 ]. However, a longitudinal study in patients with panic disorder found weight gain after one year of fluoxetine use [ 50 ]. Most RCTs in our review were under 12 months in duration, which may explain the discrepancy. Our analysis also found significant reductions in FBS and HbA1c with fluoxetine treatment, with more pronounced effects observed in obese individuals. Fluoxetine’s anorectic properties may contribute to these improvements, potentially through mechanisms involving muscle glycogen synthesis and activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway [ 14 ]. Importantly, some studies reported improvements in glycemic control independent of weight loss [ 51 ]. This underscores the dual benefit of weight reduction and metabolic regulation in fluoxetine-treated individuals. Compared with established anti-obesity medications such as semaglutide, which has demonstrated weight reductions exceeding 10–15% of initial body weight in long-term trials [ 52 ], the weight loss associated with fluoxetine (~ 2 kg) is modest. Semaglutide has also shown substantial and sustained improvements in glycemic control [ 53 ], whereas the benefits of fluoxetine appear more limited and time-dependent. These contrasts underscore the importance of considering both efficacy and mechanism of action when evaluating pharmacologic interventions for obesity and metabolic dysfunction. Notably, while the most pronounced weight loss was observed in shorter-duration trials (≤ 12 weeks), greater improvements in HbA1c emerged in longer trials (> 12 weeks). This temporal discrepancy may reflect differential mechanisms: early appetite suppression and reduced energy intake may drive initial weight reduction, whereas improvements in glycemic control may develop later through enhanced insulin sensitivity or central glucose regulation independent of weight loss. Further mechanistic studies are warranted to clarify these pathways. Given the significant health risks associated with untreated obesity, a broad range of interventions, including pharmacologic options, should be considered. Although lifestyle modification remains the cornerstone of treatment, it is often insufficient on its own. While fluoxetine is not approved as a weight-loss medication, its modest effects on weight and glycemic control suggest a potential adjunctive role when combined with behavioral interventions in select populations. Although a few trials in this review lasted up to one year, additional long-term studies with larger sample sizes are needed to determine the durability of these effects and assess long-term safety. Clinical implications Although the pooled analysis demonstrated statistically significant reductions in BW and glycemic indices with fluoxetine, the magnitude of effect (e.g., ~ 2 kg weight loss) is modest. Furthermore, the substantial heterogeneity across trials raises concerns about the generalizability and clinical significance of these findings. Accordingly, fluoxetine’s role in managing obesity and related metabolic markers should be interpreted with caution and may be best considered for select subgroups or as part of a comprehensive therapeutic strategy. Limitations There is a lack of long-term studies (≥ 1 year) assessing the sustained effects of fluoxetine on obesity and related biomarkers. Considerable heterogeneity across trials further reduces the certainty and generalizability of the findings. Although the included studies reported no industry funding, the possibility of sponsorship or publication bias cannot be completely ruled out. We attempted to explore this through funnel plots and Egger’s test; however, the limited number of trials for certain outcomes reduced the reliability of these analyses. Future meta-analyses incorporating unpublished data may provide a more robust assessment. Conclusion Fluoxetine was associated with modest but statistically significant reductions in BW, FBS, and HbA1c in overweight and obese individuals. The greatest weight loss was observed at doses ≥ 60 mg/day over shorter durations (≤ 12 weeks), whereas larger reductions in HbA1c were noted in longer trials (> 12 weeks) at similar dosages. However, these effects are relatively small compared with other pharmacologic treatments for obesity, such as GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., semaglutide), which produce greater and more sustained weight loss and improvements in glycemic control. Considerable heterogeneity among studies, along with limited data on long-term outcomes and adverse effects, warrants caution in interpreting these findings. Future research should focus on well-designed, long-term RCTs evaluating fluoxetine’s metabolic effects in non-depressed overweight and obese individuals, as most existing studies include participants with comorbid depression. Additionally, rigorous assessment and reporting of adverse effects, including potential impacts on mood, sleep, and lipid profiles, are essential to fully characterize the risk–benefit profile of fluoxetine in this context. . documents.title: The Effects of Exercise on Inhibitory Function Interventions for Patients With Major Depressive Disorder (MDD): A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Systematic Review of The effects of exercise on inhibitory function interventions for patients with major depressive disorder.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, EMbase, The Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Database, and China Science and Technology Journal Database (CQVIP) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating the impact of exercise on inhibitory function in MDD patients, from database inception to July 2024. Two researchers independently evaluated the quality of the included studies using the Risk of Bias (ROB 2.0) tool. Evidence quality was assessed with the GRADE profiler software, and effect sizes were combined using Stata 17.0 software to create forest plots, test for publication bias, and perform sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: A total of nine RCTs involving 1038 participants from six countries, published between 2001 and 2022, were included. The average age of participants in both the experimental and control groups was 45 years. Meta-analysis results indicated that exercise significantly improves inhibitory function in MDD patients, with a combined effect size (SMD = 0.48, 95% CI = 0.18-0.77, p < 0.001). Subgroup analysis showed that exercise had a statistically significant effect on inhibitory control in MDD patients, with an effect size (SMD = 0.563, p < 0.001). Regarding exercise elements, other types of exercise (resistance exercise RE, mixed exercise ME), duration greater than 45 min, intervention period of ≤12 weeks, frequency of two times per week, and low intensity were found to be more effective, all with statistical significance (SMD = 0.863, p < 0.001; SMD = 0.936, p < 0.001; SMD = 0.525, p = 0.002; SMD = 0.682, p = 0.004; SMD = 0.94, p = 0.00).
CONCLUSION: Based on the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) classification systems, a research framework for exercise interventions on executive function in MDD patients was constructed, demonstrating that exercise can improve inhibitory function in MDD with high evidence quality. Our study found that other types of exercise (RE or ME), intervention duration of >45 min, intervention period of ≤12 weeks, frequency of two times per week, and low intensity are more effective for improving inhibitory function in MDD patients. While the overall methodological quality of the literature was good, high heterogeneity existed among studies. Subgroup analysis suggested that sources of heterogeneity included measurement tools, exercise types, exercise intensity, duration, and frequency. Sensitivity analysis indicated that exercise duration and period might be causes of heterogeneity. This study has some limitations as the included literature did not consider disease duration, depression severity, or categorize age groups. However, the findings provide strong evidence for clinical practice and future research on the beneficial effects of exercise on inhibitory function in MDD patients.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: CRD42023480371.

Trial Registration CRD42023480371 Keywords: exercise, depression, inhibitory functions, systematic review status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Revised 2024 Sep 10; Received 2024 Mar 8; Accepted 2024 Oct 18; Collection date 2025 Jan. 1. Introduction Depression, also known as depressive disorder, is a mental disorder characterized by high morbidity, a high clinical cure rate but low treatment acceptance rate, and a high relapse rate (Zhang Shen‐Shuai et al. 2023 ). Typical symptoms include depressed mood, loss of interest or pleasure, and in severe cases, self‐harm or suicidal thoughts and behaviors (Wang et al. 2024 ). According to the World Health Organization, around 350 million people globally suffer from depression, leading to up to 1 million suicides each year. By 2030, depression is expected to become the leading cause of the global disease burden (Miret et al. 2013 ; Tian et al. 2013 ). As the prevalence of depression increases, it will impose a significant societal burden in the future (Peng et al. 2015 ). Impaired inhibitory functioning is a key feature of depression (Semkovska et al. 2019 ). Rock et al. ( 2013 ) reported that approximately two‐thirds of depressed individuals exhibit deficits in inhibitory functioning. Inhibitory functioning, as one of the important indicators of the development of higher order cognitive functioning (Sun Wenjing and Di 2012 ), plays an important role between cognitive bias and cognitive impairment in depressive symptomatic groups, and deficits in inhibitory functioning have become a common clinical manifestation in most patients with mental disorders. Inhibitory functioning primarily refers to the blocking of access to information that may be partially activated that is not relevant to the target and the inhibition of stimuli that are not relevant to the task at hand (Depression Research Group 2020 ). Research (Amatriain‐Fernández, García‐Noblejas, and Budde 2021 ) suggests that individuals with depressive symptoms have significant deficits in inhibitory functioning, which may be related to cognitive and emotional symptoms in individuals with depressive symptoms. It has been shown that depressed individuals tend to perform poorly on the Stroop task, possibly due to difficulties in suppressing attention to negative words in this population (Gotlib and Joormann 2010 ). Additionally, depressed individuals also show difficulties with response inhibition in the Go/No‐Go task and the Stop Signal task, which may be related to their ability to regulate their emotions (Joormann 2010 ). Exercise therapy has been one of the important non‐pharmacological interventions in antidepressant treatment in recent years, showing favorable antidepressant effects (Harvey et al. 2018 ) and an improved inhibitory functioning (Brush et al. 2022 ), but the specific effect of the impact has been inconsistent. A cross‐sectional study found a strong interrelationship between exercise participation, behavioral inhibition, and depressive symptoms, with exercise participation increasing behavioral activation systems and improving depressive symptoms (Fang et al. 2022 ). In longitudinal experiments (Hu et al. 2020 ; Miller et al. 2020 ), it was found that patients' physical fitness improved after exercise, which led to improvements in inhibitory functioning. Systematic evaluations and meta‐analytic studies have shown that exercise has the effect of significantly improving inhibitory functioning in depressed patients (Kvam et al. 2016 ). Even low‐intensity exercises like walking and yoga have been found to positively affect depression (Cramer et al. 2013 ). However, some studies argue that physical exercise does not significantly impact inhibitory functioning in adult depressed patients compared to controls (Contreras‐Osorio et al. 2022 ). Based on this, combing through previous studies, we know that there is impaired inhibitory functioning in the depressed population and that exercise is an effective means of improving depression, but the total effect on inhibitory functioning in MDD is still controversial. Second, we found that previous studies did not have subgroup analyses based on elements such as exercise duration, exercise period, and exercise frequency, and the optimal intervention program needs to be further explored. Therefore, the present study will summarize and extract the evidence from previous randomized controlled trials and conduct a meta‐analysis of the inhibitory function of exercise in patients with depression to investigate whether there is a “dose effect” of the five elements of exercise on each outcome indicator. This will provide a more accurate exercise intervention program for clinical practice and future researchers to improve the inhibitory function of patients with depression. 2. Method This study follows the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses) guidelines to ensure research transparency (Page et al. 2021b ). The study protocol has been registered on PROSPERO ( https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/ ) with registration number CRD42023480371. 2.1. Literature Search Strategy The study followed the requirements of the Systematic Reviews 2020 (Page et al. 2021a ) version and the guidelines of PRISMA 2020 (Radua 2021 ). Randomized controlled trials of exercise on inhibitory function in depressed patients were searched independently by two researchers using a computer to search seven major databases, China Knowledge, Wanfang, Wipro, PubMed, Embase, The Cochrane Libraryhe, and Web of Science, with the search date of each database established until July 2024. The search was conducted by combining subject terms with free words, using the Boolean symbols “AND” and “OR” for combinatorial concatenation, and was determined after repeated pre‐testing. EndNote 20 was used for initial screening, and then the full text was read for fine screening. In case of disagreement between the two researchers, the decision was discussed with a third researcher. This was supplemented by tracking down relevant systematic reviews and references to the included literature. The search procedure for each search library is shown in the Appendix . The Chinese search terms included “exercise/aerobic exercise/anaerobic exercise/resistance training/strength training/ball sports/physical and mental exercises/martial arts/yoga/depression/depression/inhibitory function/cognitive function/cognition/executive function/inhibitory/control,” and the English search terms included “Exercise/Aerobic exercise/physical exercise/resistance training/training/physical activity/sport/Anaerobic sports/Ball sports/Physical and Mental Exercise/Martial Arts/yoga/Depression/Depressive disorder/Depressive symptom/Emotional depression/Depressive neurosis/Endogenous depression/Unipolar depression/Inhibition function/Cognition/Cognitive performance/Cognitive/executive function/Randomized controlled trial/Randomized/controlled/Trial.” 2.2. Literature Eligibility Criteria The inclusion criteria were based on the PICOS framework to systematically evaluate and analyze the effects of exercise on inhibitory function in depressed patients, aligning with the International Classification of Disease (ICD) and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) criteria. Both experimental and control groups consisted of depressed patients meeting these diagnostic criteria. Details of exercise modalities and outcome indicators are provided in the Appendix . Exclusion criteria included non‐depressed patients, inconsistent intervention content, non‐extractable data, and non‐research literature types such as reviews or conference papers. 2.3. Data Extraction Extracted information included basic study details (author, year, nationality, age, and sample size), experimental characteristics (exercise type, intensity, duration, and frequency), and outcome indicators. Missing or unclear data were requested from original authors via email. Authors declared no conflicts of interest. 2.4. Quality Assessment The quality of the literature was assessed using the latest revised version of the Cochrane risk of bias assessment tool (ROB 2.0) (Cumpston et al. 2019 ; Zhu Tao et al. 2022 ), with two researchers conducting the quality evaluation independently. For randomized controlled trials (RCTs), a score of “Low” in all domains indicated a low risk of bias. If at least one domain was rated “Some concerns” and none were rated “High risk,” it was classified as having a moderate risk of bias. If at least one domain was rated “High risk,” it was considered a high risk of bias. In case of disagreement, a third researcher made the final decision. 2.5. Evaluation of Quality of Evidence for Outcomes The GRADE profiler software was used to evaluate the quality of evidence based on five downgrading factors: publication bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and study limitations. Evidence was categorized into four grades: high, intermediate, low, and very low. Quality ratings were independently conducted by two researchers, with a third researcher resolving any disagreements. 2.6. Statistical Methods Stata 17.0 software was used for effect size combination, publication bias, and subgroup analysis. Cohen's d was used for effect sizes, adjusting for measurement tool direction inconsistencies. Effect sizes were categorized as small (<0.2), small‐to‐medium (0.20–0.49), medium (0.50–0.79), and large (≥0.8) (Jacob 1992 ). Heterogeneity was measured using the I 2 statistic, with thresholds of 25%, 50%, and 75% indicating low, medium, and high heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins et al. 2003 ). A random effects model was used for high heterogeneity; otherwise, a fixed effects model was applied. 3. Results 3.1. Literature Search Results We identified 11,417 articles in PubMed, 2515 in The Cochrane Library, 1702 in Embase, 3341 in Web of Science, 1549 in CQVIP, 818 in CNKI, and 729 in Wanfang. After removing 4511 duplicates, 6793 articles were excluded based on title and abstract screening in EndNote. Following full‐text reading, six articles were inaccessible, 23 had non‐extractable data, 42 did not meet outcome criteria, seven lacked blank controls, and 27 were non‐exercise interventions. Eight articles were included in the meta‐analysis, as shown in Figure 1 . FIGURE 1 Literature retrieval process. 3.2. Characteristics of Included Literature As shown in Tables 1 and 2 , this meta‐analysis included eight studies (Bruchle et al. 2021 ; Hoffman et al. 2008 ; Imboden et al. 2020 ; Khatri et al. 2001 ; Krogh et al. 2012 ; Olson et al. 2017 ; Leleikiene et al. 2018 ; I. Zhang et al. 2022 ), encompassing nine RCTs. The studies were published between 2001 and 2022 and involved a total of 1038 depressed patients, with 563 in the experimental group and 475 in the control group. All subjects were diagnosed with depression, and the forms of exercise included aerobic exercise (AE), resistance training (RE), stretching (STM), and multiform exercise (ME). The intervention duration was mostly around 45 min, with the longest being 90 min (including time for warm‐up and relaxation exercises, with actual exercise duration around 30 min). The frequency of interventions was up to three times per week, with the longest intervention period being 16 weeks and the shortest 3 weeks. Exercise intensity was categorized according to the American College of Sports Medicine (Armstrong et al. 2006 ) based on maximum heart rate (HRmax) into high, medium, and low intensity. The outcome measures focused on inhibitory function, assessed using three tools: the Stroop test, the Go/No‐Go test, and the Flanker test. Quality Assessment of Included Literature The risk of bias for each study was evaluated using the RoB 2.0 tool. Green means low risk of bias, yellow means moderate risk, and red means high risk. The total quality of each article is shown in the overall column. The results indicated that one study had a low risk of bias, three studies had a medium risk, and the remaining four studies had a high risk of bias, as depicted in Figure 2 . FIGURE 2 Methodological quality assessment included in the study ( n = 8). 3.4. Meta‐Analysis Results As shown in Figure 3 , the nine included studies (Bruchle et al. 2021 ; Hoffman et al. 2008 ; Imboden et al. 2020 ; Khatri et al. 2001 ; Krogh et al. 2012 ; Olson et al. 2017 ; Leleikiene et al. 2018 ; I. Zhang et al. 2022 ) involving 1038 patients demonstrated effect sizes (Hedges's g ) with a 95% confidence interval (CI). The size of the plotted squares reflects the statistical weight of each study. Blue squares represent individual studies, green diamonds represent summarized results, and the forest plots indicate that the results favored the experimental group. Meta‐analysis revealed significant heterogeneity ( I 2 = 80.38%), and a random‐effects model was used to merge the data. A total of 20 effect sizes were included, resulting in a combined effect size of 0.48 (95% CI [0.18–0.77], p = 0.00), indicating that exercise significantly improved inhibitory function in depressed patients compared to the control group. FIGURE 3 Forest diagram of the inhibitory function of exercise on patients with depression. 3.5. Sensitivity Analysis To determine whether the heterogeneity among studies was caused by a single study, a sensitivity analysis was performed by systematically excluding individual studies. The combined effect size of exercise on inhibitory function in patients with depression across all studies was SMD = 0.48 (95% CI: 0.18–0.77, P < 0.001, I 2 = 80.38%). After excluding individual studies, the range of the combined effect size SMD remained between 0.21 and 0.56, and the I 2 range remained between 79.64% and 83.33%, with p values consistently below 0.001. The results indicated that the data sensitivity of the study was relatively low, and the meta‐analysis results were stable and reliable. See Figure 4 for details. FIGURE 4 Sensitivity analysis of inhibitory function of exercise on patients with depression. 3.6. Subgroup Analysis To further explore the potential causes of heterogeneity, a subgroup analysis of potential moderator variables was conducted. 3.7. Measurement Tools The subgroup analysis results show that, within the meta‐analysis, the inhibitory control measurement tools were categorized into three types. The Stroop task had the largest effect size, reaching a moderate effect size (SMD = 0.578), followed by the Flanker task (SMD = 0.535), and the Go/No‐Go task showed a small effect size (SMD = 0.348). This indicates statistically significant differences, suggesting that various testing tools may assess different components of inhibitory function differently. 3.7.1. Mean Age The mean age was categorized into two groups: >45 years and ≤45 years. It was found that there was statistical significance in the group with a mean age ≤45 years (SMD = 0.661, p = 0.002) (Hoffman et al. 2008 ; Khatri et al. 2001 ; Leleikiene et al. 2018 ; I. Zhang et al. 2022 ). 3.7.2.
